cases.holding: Because the juvenile court's order contained inconsistent findings about whether ICWA applied and whether active efforts and the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt serious-damage element were established, the Supreme Court retained jurisdiction and remanded for clear findings before any termination could stand.
cases.quote: Without consistent and clear factual findings supporting the application of ICWA and North Dakota heightened review for Indian families we are unable to determine the remaining issues raised by A.L.

relevance.INP-11: Holds that a juvenile court must make explicit, internally consistent findings that ICWA (and N.D.C.C. ch. 27-20.3-19, North Dakota's codification) applies before proceeding on an Indian child.
relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that foster-care placement and removal of an Indian child trigger ICWA's active-efforts finding, which must appear in the court's order.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination of parental rights to an Indian child cannot be affirmed without findings on active efforts and the beyond-a-reasonable-doubt serious-damage element.
relevance.FAIL-01: Illustrates appellate reversal/remand of a juvenile court order for defective and inconsistent findings.

cases.holding: Clear and convincing evidence supported the state-law grounds and the finding that active efforts had been made and failed, but because nothing in the record satisfied ICWA's requirement of proof beyond a reasonable doubt including qualified expert witness testimony, the court retained jurisdiction and remanded for a hearing limited to that ICWA requirement.
cases.quote: When Indian children are involved in proceedings such as this, state and federal law create a dual burden of proof for the party seeking termination of parental rights.

relevance.INP-11: States North Dakota's dual burden of proof whenever the child is an Indian child, tying state deprivation proof to ICWA's added federal proof.
relevance.OUT-02: Termination cannot be entered without qualified expert witness testimony establishing likely serious emotional or physical damage beyond a reasonable doubt.
relevance.ACT-03: Active efforts to prevent the breakup of the Indian family must be proven before foster-care placement or termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification efforts in an ICWA case are measured by the heightened active-efforts standard rather than ordinary reasonable efforts.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding incarceration alone does not prove abandonment but prognostic evidence of a long-continuing inability to care for the children satisfied both the state clear-and-convincing standard and ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt requirement.
cases.quote: While incarceration, by itself, does not establish abandonment of a child for purposes of terminating parental rights

relevance.OUT-02: Governs termination cases involving an incarcerated parent: imprisonment alone is not abandonment, but prognostic evidence of prolonged inability to parent will support termination.
relevance.INP-11: Applies ICWA's dual burden where the children are tribal members, requiring proof beyond a reasonable doubt of likely serious emotional or physical damage.
relevance.OUT-01: Shows how a court weighs a parent's inability, during incarceration, to make reunification realistic within the child's timeframe.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the findings that the child was deprived, that the causes and conditions of deprivation were likely to continue, and that continued deprivation would probably cause serious harm were each supported by clear and convincing evidence and were not clearly erroneous.
cases.quote: termination of parental rights requires satisfaction of a three-pronged test which the party petitioning for termination must prove by clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: States North Dakota's three-element termination test and the clear-and-convincing burden carried by the petitioning agency.
relevance.DEC-05: Defines what the agency must ultimately be able to prove when it files a petition seeking termination rather than temporary custody.
relevance.OUT-05: A failure of proof on any one of the three elements requires denial of the petition.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of both parents' rights, holding the juvenile court did not clearly err in finding that social services made the reasonable efforts required by statute to reunify the family before termination.
cases.quote: This Court has recognized that juvenile court findings regarding whether the State made reasonable efforts to reunify children with parents is reviewed under the clearly erroneous standard.

relevance.ACT-02: Court-ordered service plans are measured by the statutory reasonable-efforts definition, and the sufficiency of those efforts is a finding reviewed for clear error.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification must be pursued with due diligence using appropriate and available services before the state may seek termination.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary and agency-offered services count toward the reasonable efforts the state must show it made.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports resolving cases with services short of removal where due diligence can meet the family's needs.
relevance.PMC-01: Provides the state-court measure of the reasonable-efforts performance that federal CFSR review also tracks.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding that concurrent planning as applied by the county — pursuing reunification and permanent placement at the same time under N.D.C.C. § 27-20-32.2 — did not violate the mother's due process rights or her right to a fair hearing.
cases.quote: We conclude the concurrent planning as applied by Cass County did not violate S.D.'s due process rights

relevance.ACT-02: Approves concurrent planning: an agency may pursue a reunification service plan while simultaneously planning for permanency.
relevance.OUT-01: Confirms that reunification efforts remain required even while the agency plans an alternative permanent placement.
relevance.ACT-01: Voluntary services offered during concurrent planning satisfy the statutory efforts requirement without offending due process.
relevance.DEC-06: Supports front-end service engagement without abandoning the option of later permanency planning.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the juvenile court correctly applied the law and that clear and convincing evidence supported findings of deprivation, likely continuation of the causes of deprivation, resulting harm, and reasonable reunification efforts.
cases.quote: These elements must be established by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: Restates that each statutory element of termination must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
relevance.ACT-02: The agency's court-ordered services were reviewed as part of the reasonable-efforts finding supporting termination.
relevance.OUT-01: Reunification failed only after clear and convincing proof that the causes of deprivation would not be remedied.
relevance.DEC-05: Defines the proof the agency must marshal when it petitions to move from temporary custody to termination.
relevance.PMC-01: Supplies the state-court benchmark for the reasonable-efforts determinations federal reviewers audit.

cases.holding: The court reversed the order continuing a guardianship of a child and remanded, because the juvenile court applied a best-interests analysis without first expressly finding the exceptional circumstances required before a child is kept in a non-parent's custody.
cases.quote: The juvenile court's order does not expressly consider or mention exceptional circumstances.

relevance.OUT-03: Guardianship may be continued over a parent's objection only after an express exceptional-circumstances finding that triggers the best-interests analysis.
relevance.ACT-04: Placement of a child with a relative guardian rather than the parent requires the exceptional-circumstances showing, not merely a comparison of homes.
relevance.FAIL-01: Example of appellate reversal where the lower court omitted a legally required finding.
relevance.OUT-04: Addresses a guardianship structured to last until the child turns eighteen, the outer bound of juvenile-court permanency in North Dakota.
relevance.INP-05: Arose from a parent's own request to the court to review the guardianship she had earlier agreed to.

cases.holding: The court reversed the denial of a mother's motion to terminate a voluntary guardianship and remanded, holding the parent must first show by a preponderance that the impediments prompting the guardianship are gone, after which the non-parent bears a preponderance burden to overcome the parental presumption, a voluntarily created guardianship itself constituting exceptional circumstances that triggers best-interests review.
cases.quote: the natural parent must initially prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the impediments leading to the creation of the guardianship have been removed.

relevance.OUT-03: Sets the burdens of proof governing creation and termination of a minor's guardianship as a permanency arrangement.
relevance.ACT-04: Governs kin and third-party caregivers who hold guardianship, requiring them to justify continued custody against the parental presumption.
relevance.INP-05: Applies to families who voluntarily request a guardianship and later ask to have the child returned.
relevance.DEC-06: Illustrates the voluntary, non-petition route by which families place children with kin instead of entering a court deprivation case.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of H.G.C.
cases.holding: The court affirmed an order terminating a father's parental rights for abandonment under N.D.C.C. § 14-15-19(3)(a) in connection with a stepparent adoption, holding the district court's abandonment findings were not clearly erroneous.
cases.quote: A parent's intent to abandon may be inferred from the parent's conduct.

relevance.OUT-02: Supplies the abandonment ground by which parental rights may be terminated inside an adoption action, without a dependency case.
relevance.OUT-03: Distinguishes permanency achieved by adoption from guardianship, showing what a non-parent petitioner must prove when consent is withheld.
relevance.INP-05: Arises from a private family petition rather than an agency report.

cases.holding: The court reversed a domestic violence protection order and remanded because the referee's findings were too conclusory to show actual or imminent domestic violence proven by a preponderance of the evidence.
cases.quote: a party seeking a domestic violence protection order must prove actual or imminent domestic violence by a preponderance of the evidence

relevance.ACT-05: States the burden and required findings for a protective order used to remove an abuser or bar contact instead of removing the child.
relevance.FAIL-01: Shows a reviewing court vacating a protective order entered without adequate findings.
relevance.OUT-05: Demonstrates dismissal or vacatur where the record does not support the alleged danger.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of the mother's parental rights, holding the petitioner proved by clear and convincing evidence that the children were deprived, that the causes of deprivation were likely to continue, and that the children would probably suffer serious harm.
cases.quote: To terminate a parent's rights, the children must first be deprived.

relevance.OUT-02: Makes a prior or contemporaneous deprivation finding an indispensable predicate to termination.
relevance.DEC-05: Confirms that the deprivation adjudication is the gateway decision on which later petitions depend.
relevance.DEC-03: The court treats formal adjudicated deprivation, not an agency label, as the finding with legal consequences.

cases.holding: The court affirmed, holding that a requester alleging an open-records violation must give the public entity notice that describes, paraphrases, or cites the provision violated and the facts constituting the violation, and a letter merely asking the attorney general to decide whether a violation occurred did not do so.
cases.quote: the notice must describe, paraphrase, or cite to the statutory requirement alleged to have been violated and generally describe the facts alleged to constitute the violation

relevance.PMC-05: Defines what a citizen must state to trigger enforcement of North Dakota's open-records law against a public entity.
relevance.FAIL-06: Establishes the procedural notice a requester must satisfy before a disclosure failure becomes actionable.
relevance.PMC-02: Sets the mechanics for obtaining public records used in independent financial or performance review.
relevance.PMC-03: Records requests of this kind are the practical tool for testing whether review bodies are operating and reporting.
relevance.PMC-04: Applies to requests for fatality-review material held by public entities.
relevance.PMC-06: Governs the records-access route on which any external analysis of agency data depends.
relevance.INP-09: Open-records litigation is a principal external oversight trigger available to citizens.
relevance.FAIL-03: Shows the state-law transparency mechanism available when federal compliance data is withheld.

cases.holding: The court reversed a conviction, holding a four-year-old's videotaped Children's Advocacy Center forensic interview conducted with police involvement was testimonial, and playing it to the jury without an opportunity to cross-examine the available child violated the Sixth Amendment right of confrontation.
cases.quote: Statements made to non-government questioners acting in concert with or as an agent of the government are likely testimonial statements

relevance.DEC-02: Forensic interviews conducted during a child-abuse investigation with police involvement are treated as government questioning with constitutional consequences.
relevance.INP-03: Describes the law-enforcement referral pathway into a Children's Advocacy Center interview and its legal limits.
relevance.INP-07: Medical findings and the child's statements to providers were the investigative trigger and are handled differently from agency-directed interviews.
relevance.INP-08: Guides how statements a child makes to non-government adults are classified once government actors become involved.
relevance.INP-01: Shows the route from a report of suspected abuse to a coordinated law-enforcement and agency interview.
relevance.ACT-06: Involves the emergency medical examination of a child suspected of sexual abuse and the evidentiary use of what it produced.

cases.holding: The court affirmed transfer of a termination proceeding from state juvenile court to the Turtle Mountain Tribal Court under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(b), holding the county failed to carry its burden of showing good cause to deny transfer and that applying ICWA to the child was not unconstitutional.
cases.quote: The burden of establishing good cause to deny a transfer is upon the party opposing the transfer.

relevance.INP-11: Governs ICWA transfer motions: absent parental objection, the state court must transfer unless the opposing party proves good cause not to.
relevance.FAIL-05: Rejects the constitutional attack on applying ICWA to an Indian child, foreclosing a discrimination theory against ICWA's tribal preferences.
relevance.ACT-04: Tribal jurisdiction and ICWA preferences shape where an Indian child may be placed once transfer occurs.

cases.holding: The court reversed a default termination of parental rights and remanded, holding a parent who had responded to the petition could not have her rights terminated without evidence, and that the court could not rely on prior-proceeding records without satisfying the requirements for judicial notice and affording an opportunity to be heard.
cases.quote: In parental termination proceedings, due process requires clear and convincing evidence before parental rights may be terminated.

relevance.FAIL-01: Leading North Dakota example of a court vacating a termination entered without evidence or adequate process.
relevance.OUT-05: A petition unsupported by evidence at the hearing cannot produce a valid order and must be revisited.
relevance.DEC-05: Filing a petition does not relieve the agency of proving its allegations with evidence at hearing.
relevance.INP-04: Addresses how a court may and may not use the record of earlier court-supervised proceedings against a parent.

cases.case_name: Raboin v. North Dakota Department of Human Services
cases.holding: The court held that a Department determination of probable cause to believe child abuse is indicated affects legal rights and is an appealable final order, and that on this record the determination was not supported by a preponderance of the evidence, reversing and remanding with directions to vacate the probable-cause finding.
cases.quote: We conclude there is a statutory right of appeal to the courts from the Department's finding of probable cause to believe child abuse or neglect is indicated.

relevance.DEC-03: Leading North Dakota authority on the agency's substantiated ('probable cause indicated') finding, the administrative hearing that reviews it, and the parent's right to judicial review.
relevance.DEC-01: Describes the investigation-to-determination sequence, including the decision not to indicate abuse.
relevance.INP-10: Explains how a report of suspected abuse is investigated and escalated to a formal departmental determination under ch. 50-25.1.
relevance.FAIL-01: The court reversed the agency determination outright and ordered it vacated, the paradigm of judicial correction of a CPS finding.
relevance.PMC-05: Notes that child-abuse reports filed with the court and index are made confidential and exempt from public access under the open records law.
relevance.FAIL-06: Delineates the statutory confidentiality that limits disclosure of child-abuse records.
relevance.INP-01: The proceeding began with a mandated report investigated by county social services under N.D.C.C. § 50-25.1-05.
relevance.INP-02: Applies equally to reports from non-mandated reporters processed through the same investigative track.
relevance.INP-06: The intake-to-investigation machinery described applies to hotline and anonymous reports.
relevance.INP-07: The abuse allegations arose from observations reported about the children's physical condition.
relevance.INP-08: Reports originating with school and community observers enter the same ch. 50-25.1 process.
relevance.DEC-02: Sets out the department's duty to investigate an accepted report and then determine whether abuse is indicated.
relevance.PMC-02: Judicial review of agency determinations supplies a record external auditors can use.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports independent review of how the department resolves complaints about its own investigations.
relevance.OUT-05: Shows the result when an agency finding cannot be sustained on the evidence: the finding is vacated.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming dismissal of North Dakota parents' § 1983 suit against a social worker and others, the court recognized the parents' substantive due process interest in familial integrity but held that officials pursuing a child-abuse investigation retain qualified immunity when their actions rest on a reasonable suspicion of child abuse.
cases.quote: We have long recognized that parents have a liberty interest in familial relationships and have an important substantive due process right to control the care and custody of their children.

relevance.FAIL-02: Binding Eighth Circuit authority arising from North Dakota on when interference with family integrity during a CPS investigation is actionable and when qualified immunity defeats the claim.
relevance.DEC-04: Measures an emergency intervention decision against the reasonable-suspicion standard that governs caseworker immunity.
relevance.INP-12: Defines the constitutional interest that protective custody intrudes upon in North Dakota's federal circuit.
relevance.ACT-05: Shows that orders restricting a parent's contact are tested against the parental liberty interest.

cases.case_name: K.D. v. County of Crow Wing
cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: Affirming summary judgment for county and city defendants, the court held that removal of a child without a court order is constitutionally permitted only where continued parental custody poses an imminent threat, that officials acting on a reasonable suspicion of abuse have qualified immunity, and that after such a removal the state must promptly initiate judicial proceedings.
cases.quote: In cases in which continued parental custody poses an imminent threat to the child's health or welfare, emergency removal of children without a court order is constitutionally permitted.

relevance.DEC-04: States the imminent-threat standard that governs any decision to remove a child before a court order is obtained.
relevance.INP-12: Defines the narrow exigency permitting protective custody and the state's duty to seek prompt judicial review afterward.
relevance.FAIL-02: Describes the circumstances allowing warrantless removal as 'extremely limited,' framing when a removal becomes unlawful.
relevance.INP-03: Applies to joint police and social-services removals arising from a law-enforcement encounter.
relevance.INP-06: Governs action taken on an unverified tip where no imminent threat can be articulated.
relevance.OUT-06: Frames official liability where a child suffers harm in the course of a removal decision.
relevance.FAIL-04: Supplies the constitutional standard against which alleged official failures around a removal are judged.
relevance.ACT-06: Emergency intervention for a child's immediate health or welfare is permitted only on the imminent-threat showing.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: The court affirmed qualified immunity for child-protection workers who issued a founded child-abuse report and placed a caregiver on the state abuse registry before interviewing her, holding that any right to be heard before that interim finding was not clearly established.
cases.quote: We therefore affirm the district court's grant of summary judgment to the defendants on the basis of qualified immunity.

relevance.DEC-03: Shows how federal courts in this circuit treat due-process attacks on a substantiated finding and registry listing made before the accused adult is interviewed.
relevance.DEC-01: Illustrates the short statutory clocks that drive whether an allegation is confirmed, not confirmed, or held open on addendum.
relevance.DEC-02: Investigative duties include offering the accused an interview, and the timing of that interview was the crux of the claim.
relevance.INP-08: The children were interviewed separately at their school during the assessment.
relevance.INP-10: Tracks the escalation of an accepted report through assessment to a founded determination.
relevance.FAIL-05: Addresses the employment consequences of a registry listing, the setting in which retaliation and stigma claims arise.

cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit
cases.holding: After a child died in foster care, the court affirmed summary judgment for the caseworkers, holding that although foster placement creates a custodial relationship, liability requires conscience-shocking conduct — deliberate indifference where deliberation is practical — which the record did not establish.
cases.quote: a substantive due process violation will be found to have occurred only if the official conduct or inaction is so egregious or outrageous that it is conscience-shocking

relevance.OUT-06: Governing standard in this circuit for claims arising from a child's death or serious injury while in agency custody.
relevance.FAIL-04: Sets the deliberate-indifference threshold a family must meet to hold caseworkers liable for harm to a supervised child.
relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that placing a child in foster care creates a custodial relationship carrying constitutional duties of protection.
relevance.PMC-04: Defines the legal fault standard against which fatality-review findings are measured in litigation.
relevance.OUT-04: Duties owed to a child in state custody persist for as long as the custodial relationship lasts.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Adoption Assistance and Child Welfare Act's requirement that a state plan provide for 'reasonable efforts' to prevent removal and reunify families creates no right enforceable by beneficiaries under § 1983 or directly, leaving enforcement to the federal agency's plan-approval process.
cases.quote: We hold that the Act does not create an enforceable right on behalf of respondents.

relevance.FAIL-03: Establishes that federal child-welfare plan requirements are enforced by HHS through funding oversight, not by private suit.
relevance.PMC-01: Explains why CFSR and plan-compliance review, not litigation, is the operative federal accountability mechanism.
relevance.PMC-02: Places financial and program compliance in the hands of federal auditors rather than private enforcement.
relevance.PMC-03: Supports the role of federally required review bodies as the compliance check on state performance.
relevance.PMC-05: Because private enforcement is unavailable, transparency and disclosure become the practical accountability tool.
relevance.PMC-06: Frames why external analysis of published compliance data matters when private enforcement is foreclosed.
relevance.ACT-02: Reasonable-efforts obligations attached to court-ordered services derive from a state-plan requirement not privately enforceable.
relevance.OUT-04: Federal supports for older youth flow through the same state-plan structure this case addresses.
relevance.INP-09: Identifies federal plan review as the oversight trigger when a state falls short.
relevance.DEC-01: Federal screening and recordkeeping conditions are enforced through the plan-approval process rather than by suit.
relevance.FAIL-06: Compliance data disputes are resolved administratively, making disclosure obligations the main lever.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may irrevocably terminate parental rights, due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, striking down New York's fair-preponderance standard.
cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

relevance.OUT-02: Federal constitutional floor for the burden of proof in every termination of parental rights case.
relevance.DEC-03: Explains why an agency finding, made on a lower standard, cannot by itself support severance of the parent-child relationship.
relevance.FAIL-03: Identifies the constitutional minimum a state's termination scheme must satisfy regardless of federal funding rules.
relevance.INP-12: Underlies the heightened process owed to parents once the state moves against the family relationship.

cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not automatically require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding; the trial court decides the question case by case under the Eldridge factors, subject to appellate review, and no counsel was constitutionally required on these facts.
cases.quote: there is a right to appointed counsel only where the indigent, if he is unsuccessful, may lose his personal freedom

relevance.OUT-02: Sets the federal floor on appointed counsel in termination cases, which state statutes may and often do exceed.
relevance.FAIL-01: Supplies the framework for appellate review of a claim that a parent was wrongly denied counsel below.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that Washington's broad nonparental visitation statute, as applied to override a fit mother's decisions without any special weight given to her determination, violated her fundamental due process right to direct the care, custody, and control of her children.
cases.quote: the Due Process Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment protects the fundamental right of parents to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of their children

relevance.*: States the fundamental parental liberty interest that every state intervention at this decision point must be measured against, and requires that a fit parent's own judgment be given special weight.

cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that the Due Process Clause imposed no constitutional duty on county caseworkers to protect a child from his father's violence where the State had not taken the child into its custody, so their failure to act was not actionable under § 1983.
cases.quote: nothing in the language of the Due Process Clause itself requires the State to protect the life, liberty, and property of its citizens against invasion by private actors

relevance.OUT-06: Controls claims that the agency's failure to act caused a child's death or serious injury while the child remained at home.
relevance.FAIL-04: Limits constitutional liability for supervision failures to situations where the state has assumed custody of the child.
relevance.FAIL-02: The corollary of the removal cases: the Constitution constrains what the state does, not what it fails to do outside custody.
relevance.PMC-04: Explains why fatality review, rather than constitutional litigation, is usually the accountability route for deaths of children known to CPS.

cases.case_name: Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians v. Holyfield
cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that 'domicile' under ICWA is a matter of uniform federal law and that twins born off-reservation to parents domiciled on the reservation were themselves domiciled there, so the tribal court had exclusive jurisdiction and the state-court adoption decree had to be vacated.
cases.quote: We therefore think it beyond dispute that Congress intended a uniform federal law of domicile for the ICWA.

relevance.INP-11: Controls the threshold jurisdictional question whenever an Indian child's domicile may place the case in tribal court under 25 U.S.C. § 1911(a).
relevance.ACT-04: Underscores that ICWA protects tribal as well as parental interests, which shapes placement choices for Indian children.
relevance.FAIL-05: Explains ICWA's tribal-interest purpose, the answer to claims that its preferences are impermissible classifications.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of a mother's rights to her Yankton Sioux daughter, holding that state and federal law impose a dual burden — the state statutory elements by clear and convincing evidence and ICWA's serious-damage element beyond a reasonable doubt — and holding for the first time that ICWA's active-efforts requirement under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) need be proven only by clear and convincing evidence.
cases.quote: These state and federal provisions create a dual burden of proof for the party seeking parental termination of the parent of an Indian child

relevance.INP-11: This is the source decision, relied on by both T.F. and K.S.D., that first stated North Dakota's ICWA dual burden of proof once a case involves an Indian child, and it also sets the standard for qualified expert witnesses where no cultural bias is implicated.
relevance.ACT-03: Holds that ICWA's active-efforts showing before foster-care placement or termination must be proven by clear and convincing evidence, not beyond a reasonable doubt, and that agencies need not persist in efforts destined for failure.
relevance.OUT-01: Confirms that where an extended period of remedial and rehabilitative services has failed, a child cannot be left indefinitely between foster care and permanency while reunification is pursued further.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of C.D.
cases.holding: Reversing the dismissal of a stepmother's termination petition, the court held that although an Indian tribe's determination of its own membership and eligibility is binding and conclusive on the state court, the party asserting ICWA must produce admissible evidence of that determination, and allegations in the tribe's motions plus proof of Indian heritage and a pending enrollment application did not establish that the child was an Indian child.
cases.quote: An Indian tribe's determinations of its own membership and eligibility for membership are binding and conclusive in an ICWA proceeding.

relevance.INP-11: Supplies the threshold question in every North Dakota ICWA case: the court must first find on admissible evidence that the child is an 'Indian child' under 25 U.S.C. § 1903(4), and the burden of producing that evidence falls on the party asserting ICWA's application.
relevance.FAIL-01: Example of appellate reversal where the trial court applied ICWA's heightened standards on findings that could not support the threshold Indian-child conclusion.
relevance.FAIL-05: Explains that ICWA turns on current tribal membership rather than Indian ancestry precisely because Congress's authority creates a political and not a racial preference, which is the answer to discrimination challenges.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the juvenile court did not clearly err in finding by clear and convincing evidence that deprivation was likely to continue, that the child would suffer harm absent termination, and that the State made the reasonable efforts required by N.D.C.C. § 27-20-32.2 by offering an array of services the mother largely declined.
cases.quote: The State is not required to "exhaust every potential solution" before seeking termination of parental rights.

relevance.ACT-02: This is the direct North Dakota authority — reached indirectly in the brief through R.L.-P. — applying the statutory reasonable-efforts definition to a court-ordered service plan and reviewing the sufficiency of those services for clear error.
relevance.ACT-01: Holds that an agency satisfies its obligation by providing appropriate and available services the parent is free to accept or decline, and that a parent's refusal to participate does not make the efforts unreasonable.
relevance.PMC-01: Enumerates the concrete service array (parent aide, case management, evaluations, counseling, nursing, parenting classes) that a state court treats as reasonable efforts, which is the same performance federal CFSR reviewers audit.

cases.holding: The court reversed an award of a stepdaughter's custody to her stepfather and directed that custody be placed with her mother, holding that a court may not award custody to a third party under a best-interests test without first finding exceptional circumstances, which in every case upheld by the court had meant a psychological-parent relationship formed during the third party's actual physical custody.
cases.quote: Absent exceptional circumstances the natural parent is entitled to custody of the child even though the third party may be able to offer more amenities.

relevance.OUT-03: This is the parent case G.L. applies: guardianship or third-party custody as a permanency outcome requires a threshold exceptional-circumstances finding, and a better-resourced non-parent home is not enough.
relevance.ACT-04: Governs placement with a stepparent or other non-parent caregiver over the parent's objection, requiring the psychological-parent showing rather than a comparison of homes.
relevance.INP-04: Instructs that where a parent's fitness to provide minimally adequate care is genuinely at issue, the route is a ch. 27-20 deprivation proceeding commenced for that purpose, not a fitness ruling inside a divorce custody case.

cases.holding: The court affirmed an award of reasonable visitation to a stepfather while leaving decisionmaking and primary residential responsibility with the fit biological mother, holding that his psychological-parent relationship was an exceptional circumstance sufficient to justify that lesser intrusion on her constitutional parental rights even though no serious harm or detriment warranted transferring custody to him.
cases.quote: The existence of a psychological parent relationship can constitute exceptional circumstances justifying the placement of decisionmaking responsibility and primary residential responsibility with a third party.

relevance.OUT-03: The leading modern North Dakota statement of the parental presumption and the graduated exceptional-circumstances showing: more is required to move custody to a non-parent than to grant that person contact.
relevance.ACT-04: Fixes what a kin or de facto caregiver must establish to keep a legal relationship with the child when the parent objects, and confirms parental fitness is not the test.
relevance.INP-05: Arises from a private family proceeding in which the adults themselves asked the court to allocate responsibility for a child, with no agency report or abuse allegation.

cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of S.R.F.
cases.holding: The court affirmed a judgment terminating a mother's parental rights for abandonment under N.D.C.C. §§ 14-15-06(1)(a) and 14-15-19(3)(a) and granting the guardians' adoption petition, holding the abandonment findings were not clearly erroneous and overruling prior cases that had applied de novo review to adoption-act appeals.
cases.quote: A party seeking termination of the parent-child relationship in the context of an adoption proceeding must prove the elements necessary to support termination by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.OUT-02: This is the abandonment authority Adoption of H.G.C. quotes: it sets out the factors — contact and communication, love and affection, intent, and acceptance of parental obligations — and fixes the clear-and-convincing burden for terminating rights inside an adoption action.
relevance.OUT-03: Shows how a guardianship arrangement can convert into adoptive permanency when the parent, without justifiable cause, never moves to end the guardianship or resume care.
relevance.INP-05: Begins with a mother voluntarily placing her child with family friends and consenting to their guardianship, the front-end self-referral route, and traces what happens when she does not follow through.

cases.holding: The court affirmed an adjudication that a ten-year-old was deprived by reason of parental alienation and psychological maltreatment, holding the finding of deprivation by clear and convincing evidence was not clearly erroneous and that the juvenile court had not improperly merged the divorce-related custody dispute with the deprivation proceeding.
cases.quote: A juvenile court's finding of deprivation must be supported by clear and convincing evidence.

relevance.DEC-05: The clean citation for the burden the agency carries when it files a deprivation petition, decided the same day as T.J.L. and applied without the distortion the brief flagged elsewhere.
relevance.DEC-03: Confirms that the legally operative determination is the juvenile court's adjudication of deprivation under N.D.C.C. § 27-20-02(8)(a), reviewed for clear error, not any agency characterization.
relevance.INP-04: Addresses the case that enters the child-welfare system out of ongoing civil litigation: the district court deferred its visitation ruling to the deprivation proceeding, and the court held that ch. 27-20 hearings must be conducted separately from proceedings outside juvenile-court jurisdiction even though judicial notice of prior adjudications is permitted.
relevance.INP-12: Illustrates a disposition short of protective custody — legal custody to the Department while the child remains physically with the parent, with authority to remove if the conduct recurs.

cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of a mother's motion to withdraw her consent to termination of her parental rights, holding the motion was untimely because N.D.C.C. § 27-20-45(6) bars any challenge to a termination order more than thirty days after it is issued by a person who did not retain custody of the child.
cases.quote: The mother's motion was untimely under N.D.C.C. § 27-20-45(6) and the juvenile court did not err in denying the mother's motion to withdraw her consent.

relevance.OUT-02: Governs the voluntary route to termination: once a parent consents and the order issues, a thirty-day statutory bar forecloses reopening it on any ground, including fraud, unless the parent retained custody.
relevance.INP-05: Warns families who agree to a consensual resolution that the window to reconsider is thirty days from the order, and that another party's pending appeal does not necessarily preserve it.

cases.holding: The court retained jurisdiction and remanded for detailed ICWA findings, holding that while a qualified expert witness's preference against termination does not itself bar termination, the juvenile court's vague paraphrase of the statutory language was not the specific finding, beyond a reasonable doubt, that continued parental custody was likely to result in serious emotional or physical damage that 25 U.S.C. § 1912(f) requires.
cases.quote: A qualified expert witness's expressed preference to deny termination of parental rights does not preclude the court from making findings sufficient to satisfy ICWA and ordering termination.

relevance.INP-11: The most current North Dakota authority on the qualified-expert-witness element of ICWA: the ultimate serious-damage finding belongs to the judge, not the expert, but the court must make it explicitly and will not have it inferred from a vague reference to the statute.
relevance.FAIL-01: A remand for defective findings in an ICWA termination, driven expressly by the risk that inadequate findings expose the judgment to later collateral attack.

cases.holding: On return from its own remand, the court affirmed the juvenile court's order denying the petition to terminate the mother's parental rights and instead removing the children from her custody for nine months, deferring to the finding that the qualified expert's testimony raised a reasonable doubt whether continued custody was likely to cause serious emotional or physical damage.
cases.quote: A finding relating to a likelihood of future harm requires some prognostic evidence providing "the basis for a reasonable prediction as to future action."

relevance.INP-11: The sequel that shows how ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt standard actually operates on remand: contrary expert testimony from the tribe's qualified expert can defeat the State's proof even where the court doubts the expert's assessment.
relevance.ACT-03: Confirms that a court that declines to terminate may still order the children removed and kept in agency custody for a fixed period, here nine months, as the disposition.
relevance.OUT-05: A concrete example of a termination petition denied for failure of proof, with the denial affirmed under the clearly erroneous standard.

cases.holding: The court retained jurisdiction and remanded with instructions to issue a new order based only on the trial evidence, holding that even when the statutory elements of N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c) are established the juvenile court retains discretion whether to terminate, and that it abused that discretion by relying on evidence outside the record and on a clearly erroneous count of the child's nights in foster care.
cases.quote: Therefore, when the statutory elements to terminate parental rights are met, the court has discretion, but is not required, to terminate parental rights.

relevance.OUT-02: Current-chapter authority: it lays out both grounds under N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c) — likely-to-continue need for protection with resulting harm, and 450 of the previous 660 nights in foster care — and holds the decision to terminate is discretionary even once a ground is proven.
relevance.DEC-05: Confirms that the agency's petition must be decided on the evidentiary record made at the hearing, and that a court may not fill gaps by taking judicial notice of material outside that record.
relevance.FAIL-01: A reversal-in-substance for reliance on inadmissible evidence and erroneous findings, showing the appellate check available under the current juvenile chapter.

cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of a father's parental rights under the current juvenile chapter, holding that N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c)(2) requires only that the child have been in foster care at least 450 nights and does not require that 660 nights have elapsed since the child entered care.
cases.quote: The plain language of the statute requires the child be in care for at least 450 nights.

relevance.ACT-03: Construes the foster-care duration ground of the current chapter, fixing how the 450-of-660-nights clock is computed from the date of placement.
relevance.DEC-05: Shows the sequence under ch. 27-20.3 from placement to a child-in-need-of-protection adjudication to a permanency hearing to the termination petition, and what the agency must prove at each step.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a twelve-month extension of a child's placement in the custody of county social services, holding the findings of continuing deprivation and of reasonable efforts to reunify and to maintain family connections were not clearly erroneous, and that the custodian did not abuse its authority by keeping the child with out-of-state relatives as the permanent plan.
cases.quote: The custodian has an obligation and right to determine the nature of care, placement, and treatment of a child considering the child's best interests.

relevance.ACT-02: Sets out the statutory menu of dispositions under N.D.C.C. § 27-20-30 and the limits on extending a dispositional order, which is the mechanism by which court-ordered supervision and services continue year to year.
relevance.ACT-04: The nearest North Dakota authority on non-ICWA kinship placement: it upholds the agency's placement of the child with a paternal aunt and uncle in another state as the permanency plan and confirms the custodian's authority over placement, subject to the court's power to order the child returned if deprivation ends.
relevance.OUT-03: Identifies appointment of a fit and willing relative as legal guardian as one of the enumerated permanency dispositions available short of termination and adoption.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a two-year domestic violence protection order, holding that dismissal of an earlier petition for non-appearance did not bar a second petition alleging new incidents, and that the district court's sparse findings of assault and threatening behavior were adequate to show actual or imminent domestic violence and were not clearly erroneous.
cases.quote: A petitioner seeking a domestic violence protection order must prove "actual or imminent domestic violence" by a preponderance of evidence.

relevance.ACT-05: One of the two source decisions Niska rests on: it fixes the preponderance burden, requires specific findings of actual or imminent domestic violence, and confirms that past abuse and the history of the relationship are relevant context when a protective order is used to separate the abuser rather than remove the child.

cases.holding: The court affirmed a two-year domestic violence protection order, holding that domestic violence may be found on actual physical harm or on the infliction of fear of imminent physical harm, but never on fear alone of harm that might occur at some indefinite future time, and that the findings here met that standard.
cases.quote: We emphasize that when a finding of domestic violence is based solely on fear, the fear must be of imminent physical harm.

relevance.ACT-05: The companion source decision to Hanneman, drawing the line that a protective order cannot rest on fear of some future harm, and correcting earlier opinions that had blurred 'actual' and 'imminent' — the precise defect that produced reversal in Niska.

cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
cases.holding: The Court held that an unwed father was entitled as a matter of due process to a hearing on his fitness before his children could be taken from him, and that Illinois's presumption of unfitness for unwed fathers, while affording a hearing to every other parent, denied him equal protection.
cases.quote: We conclude that, as a matter of due process of law, Stanley was entitled to a hearing on his fitness as a parent before his children were taken from him

relevance.INP-12: The federal due-process predicate underlying every emergency or protective removal: the State must give the parent a hearing on fitness before permanently depriving him of his children, and cannot substitute a presumption for individualized proof.
relevance.DEC-04: Explains why administrative convenience and a generalized presumption cannot justify taking custody without an individualized determination about this parent.
relevance.DEC-05: Establishes that the State's petition must lead to an adjudication of the particular parent's fitness, which is the constitutional root of North Dakota's requirement that a deprivation or need-for-protection petition be proven at a hearing.
relevance.FAIL-02: Foundational § 1983-era authority on the constitutional defect in removing children from a parent without the process the Fourteenth Amendment requires.

notes: Every case listed was retrieved from CourtListener in this session and its opinion text read; each quote was machine-verified as an exact substring of the retrieved opinion text (whitespace and curly quotes normalized). No quote is taken from a syllabus, dissent, concurrence or headnote; North Dakota Supreme Court opinions in this dataset carry no syllabus, and for the U.S. Supreme Court cases the quoted sentences were confirmed to fall after the 'delivered the opinion of the Court' marker and before any dissent.

Statutory renumbering, critical for reading the older ND cases: North Dakota replaced the Uniform Juvenile Court Act (N.D.C.C. ch. 27-20, 'deprived child', termination under § 27-20-44) with ch. 27-20.3 ('child in need of protection', termination under § 27-20.3-20) effective 2021, and added a state ICWA codification at § 27-20.3-19 effective July 2021. Interest of T.J.L. (2004), In the Interest of T.F. (2004), In the Interest of N.H. (2001), Interest of J.C. (2007), Interest of A.S. (2007), Interest of J.A.H. (2014), Interest of R.L.-P. (2014) and Interest of A.L.E. (2018) state their rules under the former chapter; Interest of A.C. (2022) confirms the same clear-and-convincing burden and three-element structure carries forward under § 27-20.3-20.

No North Dakota appellate decision could be found construing the mandatory-reporter duty or the reporter-immunity provisions of N.D.C.C. ch. 50-25.1 (multiple targeted CourtListener searches for reporter duty, failure to report, and good-faith immunity returned nothing on point). INP-01, INP-02, INP-06, INP-07 and INP-08 are therefore built on Raboin (the report-to-investigation-to-determination machinery of ch. 50-25.1), State v. Blue (child forensic interviews after a report), and Eighth Circuit authority on how investigators may act on a report. A lawyer should read N.D.C.C. 50-25.1-03, -04, -05 and -09 directly; the immunity question is unlitigated in the reported North Dakota case law.

Raboin v. North Dakota Department of Human Services (1996) is the only North Dakota decision found on the agency's substantiated ('probable cause indicated') finding, the administrative appeal from it, and the confidentiality of child-abuse reports. It construes the 1990s text of N.D.C.C. 50-25.1-05.1 through -05.4 and NDAC ch. 75-03-18; counsel must verify the current statutory and rule text (including present terminology for departmental determinations and the child-abuse index) before relying on the procedural detail, though the holding that such a determination is an appealable final order remains the leading statement.

Nodes with no North Dakota authority found, carried on the federal standard and so flagged: OUT-04 (extended foster care / jurisdiction past 18 — no ND case located on Chafee or extended care; Interest of G.L. is used only because that guardianship ran to age eighteen); ACT-04 (no ND decision on statutory kinship or sibling placement preference outside ICWA); DEC-06 (no ND decision on differential or alternative response); INP-09 and PMC-01 through PMC-06 (no ND decision on CFSR, OIG audit, citizen review panels or fatality-review commissions — Suter v. Artist M. supplies the controlling rule that federal plan requirements are enforced administratively, and Mickelson v. City of Rolla supplies the state transparency mechanism). Nothing was found in any court on children missing from North Dakota foster care.

North Dakota's Court of Appeals (courtlistener id ndctapp) is effectively dormant and produced no relevant results; every state case here is a published North Dakota Supreme Court opinion. No unpublished or memorandum decision was used, and no summary affirmance was used (Interest of S.R., 2021 ND 64, surfaced in search but is a Rule 35.1(a)(2) summary affirmance and was discarded).

North Dakota sits in the Eighth Circuit, so Dornheim v. Sholes (which arose from North Dakota), K.D. v. County of Crow Wing, Webster v. Westlake, Hovick v. Patterson and James v. Friend are binding circuit precedent for § 1983 claims in North Dakota. Webster and Hovick arose from Iowa and Crow Wing, Deason and James from Minnesota and Missouri respectively; their statutory discussion is of those states' codes, but the constitutional holdings quoted here bind North Dakota federal courts. In Webster and Hovick the plaintiffs lost on qualified immunity even though (in Webster) a Fourth Amendment violation was found — families should not read those cases as promising damages.

Troxel v. Granville is a four-Justice plurality; its statement of the fundamental parental right is nonetheless the routinely cited formulation and was quoted from the opinion of the Court as written by Justice O'Connor.

Two CourtListener date fields are unreliable and were corrected from the opinion text itself: the Lassiter cluster is dated 1981-08-28 but the opinion states 'Decided June 1, 1981', and the Santosky cluster is dated 1982-02-22 but the opinion states 'Decided March 24, 1982'. The dates reported here are the dates the opinions state.

Duplicate clusters exist in CourtListener for several of these cases (for example 2022 ND 123 appears at clusters 6475836 and 8241338, and In the Interest of T.F. at 897467 and 897458). The cluster chosen in each entry is the one carrying the official reporter citation whose opinion text was actually read; a second cluster id for the same case is not an error in the source but a duplicate record.

The existing layers.case_law.key_cases entries in the ND node files are keyword-matched noise: the most frequent titles (Matter of Hansen Trust, Interest of J.C. 2025 ND 217, Interest of G.S./A.S. 2025 ND 214, Interest of A.D.-B./M.D.-B./C.B. 2025 ND 203, Interest of B.L.H. 2025 ND 207, Interest of M.P. 2025 ND 181) are recent listings with synthetic citations and, in the case of Hansen Trust, not a child-welfare matter at all. None was retained. The adoption and guardianship titles in those files were used only as search leads; of them, only cases independently retrieved and read (Adoption of H.G.C., Guardianship of Barros) appear here.

Practice point for ICWA cases in North Dakota, the state's highest-volume area of child-welfare appellate law: the dual burden (Interest of K.S.D.), the requirement of qualified expert witness testimony before termination (K.S.D., Interest of A.C.), the transfer-to-tribal-court burden on the party opposing transfer (In the Interest of A.B.), and the federal domicile rule (Holyfield) together control INP-11, ACT-03, ACT-04 and OUT-02. Since July 2021 the parallel state provision, N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-19, must be analyzed alongside 25 U.S.C. § 1912; Interest of A.C. expressly notes that the parties had framed the case under federal ICWA alone and that the state codification also applied.

Added In the Interest of M.S., 2001 ND 68, 624 N.W.2d 678 (cluster 896766) for INP-11, ACT-03 and OUT-01: it is the source decision on which both In the Interest of T.F. and Interest of K.S.D. rest their dual-burden rule, and it separately holds that ICWA's active-efforts element under 25 U.S.C. § 1912(d) need be proven only by clear and convincing evidence, a point no other case in this brief supplies.

Added In the Matter of the Adoption of C.D., 2008 ND 128, 751 N.W.2d 236 (cluster 898301) for INP-11, FAIL-01 and FAIL-05: it supplies the threshold Indian-child determination that every ND ICWA case turns on — a tribe's own membership and eligibility determination is binding and conclusive on the state court, but the party asserting ICWA must produce admissible evidence of that determination, and Indian heritage, blood quantum or a pending enrollment application is not enough.

Added In the Interest of A.B., 2009 ND 116, 767 N.W.2d 817 (cluster 898561) for ACT-02, ACT-01 and PMC-01: it is the direct reasonable-efforts authority the brief previously reached only through Interest of R.L.-P., applying the N.D.C.C. § 27-20-32.2 definition to a concrete service array and holding the State need not exhaust every potential solution before petitioning to terminate.

Added Worden v. Worden, 434 N.W.2d 341 (N.D. 1989) (cluster 1643981) for OUT-03, ACT-04 and INP-04: it is the parent case Interest of G.L. applies, holding a court may not award custody to a third party on a best-interests test without first finding exceptional circumstances, and directing that a genuine parental-fitness dispute be litigated in a ch. 27-20 deprivation proceeding rather than inside a custody case.

Added McAllister v. McAllister, 2010 ND 40, 779 N.W.2d 652 (cluster 898683) for OUT-03, ACT-04 and INP-05: the leading modern ND statement of the parental presumption and of the psychological-parent form of exceptional circumstances, including the graduated rule that granting a third party visitation requires a lesser showing than transferring residential responsibility.

Added In the Matter of the Adoption of S.R.F., 2004 ND 150, 683 N.W.2d 913 (cluster 1232354) for OUT-02, OUT-03 and INP-05: this is the abandonment authority Adoption of H.G.C. quotes verbatim, setting out the abandonment factors and the clear-and-convincing burden for terminating parental rights inside an adoption action, and it is also the decision that abolished de novo review of adoption-act appeals in favor of N.D.R.Civ.P. 52(a).

Added In the Interest of T.T., 2004 ND 138, 681 N.W.2d 779 (cluster 897465) for DEC-05, DEC-03, INP-04 and INP-12: it is the clean citation for the clear-and-convincing deprivation standard, and it additionally holds that ch. 27-20 hearings must be conducted separately from proceedings outside juvenile-court jurisdiction even though the juvenile court may take judicial notice of adjudications in a related divorce file — the only ND authority located on the civil-proceeding-to-CPS pathway at INP-04.

Added Interest of K.S.D., 2019 ND 110, 925 N.W.2d 760 (cluster 4610172) for OUT-02 and INP-05, with a correction: this decision is NOT the sequel to the ICWA remand in 2017 ND 289. It is a separate appeal by the mother about withdrawing her consent to termination, and it holds that N.D.C.C. § 27-20-45(6) bars any challenge to a termination order more than thirty days after issuance by a parent who did not retain custody.

Correction to the verifier's list and to the 2017 ND 289 entry: the actual sequel to Interest of K.S.D., 2017 ND 289 is Interest of K.S.D., 2018 ND 103, 910 N.W.2d 834 (cluster 4495908, opinion 4273161), retrieved and read in this session. On remand the juvenile court made the required qualified-expert and § 1912(f) findings and the Supreme Court affirmed — but it did so per curiam under N.D.R.App.P. 35.1(a)(2), a summary affirmance, so under this brief's stated methodology it is recorded here rather than added as a case entry. Counsel citing the 2017 retain-jurisdiction remand must cite 2018 ND 103 for the outcome.

Added Interest of K.B., 2021 ND 106, 961 N.W.2d 293 (cluster 4894387) for INP-11 and FAIL-01: the most current ND authority on ICWA's qualified-expert-witness element, holding that the ultimate serious-damage finding belongs to the judge rather than the expert, that an expert's preference against termination does not preclude termination, but that the court must make the § 1912(f) finding explicitly and the Supreme Court will not strain to infer it. The N.W.2d parallel citation is not carried in the CourtListener cluster; it was taken from the text of Interest of K.B., 2021 ND 163, read in this session.

Added Interest of K.B., 2021 ND 163 (cluster 5092497) for INP-11, ACT-03 and OUT-05: the sequel on return from that remand, affirming the juvenile court's denial of the termination petition and its nine-month removal order, and showing how contrary testimony from the tribe's qualified expert can defeat proof beyond a reasonable doubt even where the court disagrees with the expert. The Chief Justice's separate opinion at ¶¶ 8-13 argues the majority reading renders the expert requirement illusory; it was not quoted here.

Added Interest of J.C., 2024 ND 9, 2 N.W.3d 228 (cluster 9467764) for OUT-02, DEC-05 and FAIL-01: the brief's first authored authority decided under the CURRENT juvenile chapter, setting out both grounds of N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c), holding that termination remains discretionary even once a ground is proven, and reversing in substance for reliance on evidence outside the record. The N.W.3d parallel citation is not carried in the CourtListener cluster; it was taken from the text of Interest of O.F., 2024 ND 140, read in this session.

Added Interest of O.F., 2024 ND 140 (cluster 10006485) for ACT-03 and DEC-05: a published, authored opinion (Tufte, J.) construing N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c)(2) to require only 450 nights in foster care rather than 660 elapsed nights since placement. Caveat for counsel: the opinion concludes by summarily affirming under N.D.R.App.P. 35.1(a)(2) and (4), so it is a hybrid — the statutory holding at ¶¶ 6-8 is reasoned and precedential, but the affirmance carries a summary label.

Could not add Interest of H.J.J.N., 2024 ND 132 (clusters 9997735 and 10131133, opinion 10464336). It is real and was retrieved and read, but it is a three-paragraph per curiam summary affirmance under N.D.R.App.P. 35.1(a)(2) and (4) following the remand ordered in Interest of H.J.J.N., 2024 ND 70, 5 N.W.3d 775, and it states no rule of its own. It is excluded under this brief's no-summary-affirmance rule; Interest of J.C., 2024 ND 9 and Interest of O.F., 2024 ND 140 fill the current-chapter gap instead.

Added Hanneman v. Nygaard, 2010 ND 113, 784 N.W.2d 117 (cluster 898743) and Lenton v. Lenton, 2010 ND 125, 784 N.W.2d 131 (cluster 898737) for ACT-05: the two source decisions Niska v. Falconer rests on. Hanneman fixes the preponderance burden and the requirement of specific findings of actual or imminent domestic violence; Lenton draws the line that a finding based on fear alone must be fear of IMMINENT physical harm, not harm that may occur at some indefinite future time — the precise defect that produced reversal in Niska. ACT-05 no longer rests on a single derivative decision.

Added Stanley v. Illinois, 405 U.S. 645 (1972) (cluster 108497) for INP-12, DEC-04, DEC-05 and FAIL-02: the federal due-process predicate requiring a hearing on a parent's fitness before the State may take his children, and the rejection of a statutory presumption of unfitness as a substitute for individualized proof. It is relied on in the separate opinion in Guardianship of Barros and underlies North Dakota's requirement that a deprivation or need-for-protection petition be proven at a hearing.

Added In the Interest of B.B., 2010 ND 9, 777 N.W.2d 350 (cluster 2234143) for ACT-02, ACT-04 and OUT-03, found while searching to fill the kinship-placement and extended-placement gaps the brief conceded. It is the nearest North Dakota authority on non-ICWA kinship placement: it upholds the agency's placement of a child with a paternal aunt and uncle out of state as the permanency plan, confirms the custodian's authority to determine placement subject to the court's power to order the child returned, sets out the N.D.C.C. § 27-20-30 menu of dispositions including appointment of a fit and willing relative as guardian, and states the limits on extending a dispositional order. Date correction: CourtListener cluster 2234143 carries date_filed 2010-09-25, but the opinion text states 'January 12, 2010' and the duplicate cluster 8279797 carries 2010-01-12; the date reported here is 2010-01-12.

The previously empty or single-case nodes were closed as follows — INP-04 (was empty) now has Interest of J.C. 2007, Worden and T.T.; OUT-04 (was empty) now maps Interest of G.L., James v. Friend and Suter v. Artist M., all of which already carried OUT-04 relevance; INP-01 adds State v. Blue; INP-08 adds State v. These eight fills use relevance sentences that were already stated in the existing case entries but had not been reflected in node_map.

Six nodes exceed the six-case guideline: INP-11 (9), OUT-02 (9), FAIL-01 (8), DEC-05 (8), and ACT-02/ACT-03/ACT-04/OUT-01/OUT-03 sit at the cap of six. This is a genuine feature of North Dakota's published child-welfare appellate output, which concentrates overwhelmingly on ICWA compliance and on termination of parental rights. None of the listed cases is redundant: at INP-11, A.B. (2003) governs transfer, Holyfield governs domicile, C.D. governs the threshold Indian-child determination, M.S. and K.S.D. state the dual burden, K.B. (both 2021 decisions) govern qualified expert testimony, A.C. governs the consistency of findings, and T.F. applies the standard to an incarcerated parent.

Searches run in this session that returned nothing usable, recorded so the gaps are not re-litigated: no North Dakota decision was found on juvenile-court jurisdiction or foster care continuing past age eighteen (OUT-04 remains on the federal standard); no ND decision was found construing differential or alternative response (DEC-06 remains supported only by the voluntary-guardianship and concurrent-planning cases); and a targeted search of the mandatory-reporter statutes again returned only unrelated criminal appeals, confirming the earlier finding that ch. 50-25.1's reporter duty and immunity provisions are unlitigated in reported ND case law.
